verdicts.why: Arriving at a place or goal is stated plainly; the word takes no side on the goal or the one who reaches it.
Attaining something with effort is the meaning itself, not an attitude on top of it; 'reach' is the plain neighbour of 'attain'.
Handing something to someone is a bare physical act; no approval or contempt rides on choosing 'reach' over 'pass'.
Straining or striving is described, not judged; the word says nothing about whether the effort is admirable or foolish.
The end of gestation is a clinical, technical use with no attitude toward the pregnancy or the mother.
A mathematical term is a purely technical label; there is no plain neighbour it is being chosen over for effect.
A term of a logical proposition is a technical name with no judgement in it.
The architectural pillar-bust is a plain object name; nothing about the speaker's attitude is carried by it.
Directions written on a letter are named without any attitude; the word is as flat as 'letter' itself.
A sign giving a location is a neutral object; no judgement is implied by calling it an address.
A memory address in computing is a technical term with no evaluative colour at all.
The sense names a positive ability (like 'skill' or 'tact'), but that is its meaning rather than an attitude beyond it, and the sentences use it as a plain quality one can have more or less of.
A golfer's stance is a technical sporting term that describes and does not judge.
A visitor or guest is named plainly; 'company' carries no approval or dismissal of the person visiting.
A band of people gathered for some activity is described neutrally; the sentences treat 'the company' as simply those present.
A theatrical company is an organisational label with no attitude toward the performers.
A military company is a formal unit name; nothing evaluative rides on it.
A ship's company is a plain collective term for the crew, with no judgement of them.
A fire company is an organisational unit name with no evaluative colour.
A window of time is a neutral figure for an opportunity's span; it does not praise or belittle what is done in it.
A screen window is a technical computing term with no attitude in it.
A serving or wall opening is a plain physical object, the sort of word the bulk of a vocabulary is made of.
An opening that resembles a window is described by likeness alone; no judgement is attached.
A transparent panel in an envelope is a bare object name with no evaluative content.
Coating or smearing a surface is a plain action; 'apply' is if anything the more neutral neighbour of 'smear', not the loaded one.
